message.content:
In our own Solar System, **Jupiter** is the largest planet—about 1 000 times the mass of Earth and roughly 11 times its radius.

Across the entire Universe, astronomers have discovered many exoplanets that dwarf Jupiter. The record‑holder so far is an object called **HD 100546 b**, which has a mass of roughly **20–25 times that of Jupiter** (about 0.02–0.025 solar masses). That makes it more than twice as massive as the next‑largest known exoplanet, and it sits at the boundary between giant planets and brown dwarfs.

So while Jupiter remains the biggest planet in our local neighborhood, the Universe hosts exoplanets that are several times larger in mass—and even larger in size—than Jupiter itself.
